original_question: Consider a perturbation A~ f~ = g~ of an inverse problem Af = g induced by a Friedrichs operator A, where A~ is close to A and g~ is close to g in a suitable sense. Determine when the Krylov subspaces K(A, g) and K(A~, g~) stay close in the weak-gap metric dbw on closed subspaces of a separable Hilbert space, when such perturbations preserve Krylov solvability, when they destroy or create it, and what additional conclusions hold when the perturbation also preserves the Friedrichs character of the operator.
target_in_paper: Section 4, Question 6: the perturbation problem for an inverse linear problem induced by a Friedrichs operator, asking when the associated Krylov subspaces remain close in the weak-gap metric and when Krylov solvability is preserved, lost, or gained, especially under perturbations that preserve Friedrichs structure.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper's actual target. It correctly identifies that the paper is asking a perturbative question about an inverse problem Af = g induced by a Friedrichs operator, with a perturbed problem involving tilde A and tilde g; it correctly singles out the weak-gap metric as the relevant notion of closeness for Krylov subspaces; it correctly asks about persistence versus destruction/creation of Krylov solvability; and it correctly isolates the special subcase in which the perturbation preserves the Friedrichs nature of the operator/system.
missing_details: The ambient setting should be stated explicitly: a separable complex Hilbert space.

Because the weak-gap metric is defined on closed subspaces, the question should clarify that one compares the closures of the Krylov subspaces, or otherwise explicitly state that the relevant Krylov subspaces are viewed through their closures.
If A or tilde A is unbounded, the Krylov subspace K(A,g) is only defined when g belongs to the domain of every power of A; likewise tilde g must belong to the domain of every power of tilde A.
The inverse problems should be stated as solvable (for example, g in Ran(A) and tilde g in Ran(tilde A)), otherwise Krylov solvability is not yet a meaningful issue.
The Friedrichs hypothesis should be tied to the abstract framework of Section 3: A is not just any operator, but an operator of Friedrichs type (or a closed realization in that framework).
The paper phrases this as an open-ended criteria question ('when'), not as a request for a full classification or complete perturbation theory.

The strengthened subcase in the paper is not only that tilde A is again of Friedrichs type, but also, more strongly, that the perturbation may preserve the Friedrichs-system status of the whole inverse problem.
refined_question: Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space, let A be an operator of Friedrichs type in the abstract sense of Section 3, and let Af = g be a solvable inverse linear problem on H. For a perturbed solvable problem tilde A tilde f = tilde g, with tilde A close to A and tilde g close to g in some suitable sense, determine criteria under which the closed Krylov subspaces associated with (A,g) and (tilde A,tilde g) are close in the weak-gap metric d_bw, and determine when such perturbations preserve Krylov solvability of Af = g, and when they can instead destroy or create Krylov solvability. If A or tilde A is unbounded, assume g and tilde g belong to the domain of every power of the corresponding operator so that the Krylov subspaces are defined. What sharper conclusions can be obtained in the special case that the perturbation keeps tilde A within the Friedrichs class, or even preserves the full Friedrichs-system structure of the inverse problem?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 4, Question 6 almost exactly. The official question there has the same three components: weak-gap closeness of perturbed Krylov subspaces, preservation versus alteration of Krylov solvability, and the special Friedrichs-preserving perturbative regime. The immediately preceding context in Section 2.4 is the paper's own guide to how Question 6 should be read: Example 2.8 shows that perturbations can cause loss or gain of Krylov solvability; the paragraph around equation (2.11) introduces the weak-gap metric on closed subspaces; and Proposition 2.9 records a preservation mechanism under suitable weak-gap convergence assumptions. Section 3 supplies the precise abstract Friedrichs framework. One additional stand-alone detail is needed from the unbounded-operator discussion in Section 2.3: for unbounded operators, the Krylov subspace itself is only defined when the datum lies in the domain of every operator power. The paper does not prove an equivalence or a final theorem here; it leaves the matter as an open research question, so the refined version should ask for criteria rather than claim a known classification.
